background.definition: Inflammation of the conjunctiva due to allergen exposure.

list.listitem: Affects 5% to 40% of the US population, varying with geographic region; it is most common in spring and summer.

In an online survey of 500 adults and 501 children with allergic conjunctivitis, over half reported daily symptoms and 75% to 80% considered their symptoms moderate to severe. Greater treatment satisfaction was reported by those using prescription medications.
Ocular exposure to airborne or contact allergens.
Common airborne allergens include pollen from trees, grass, and weeds, as well as pet dander.

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a rare, chronic and often severe bilateral form of allergic conjunctivitis. It is considered both an IgE- and non-Ig E-mediated ocular allergic disease that usually begins during the first decade and disappears during the end of the second decade of life. Seen most often in hot, arid environments such as West Africa and the Indian subcontinent; the prevalence in Western Europe is 3.2/10,000 inhabitants based on the results of a cross-sectional survey of 3003 ophthalmologists from six countries.
It may be comorbid with atopic dermatitis.
Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.
Cross-linking of Immunoglobulin E molecules.
Mast cell degranulation.
Release of allergic and inflammatory mediators including histamine and leukotrienes.

Consumption of probiotic milk during pregnancy is associated with a slightly reduced relative risk (RR) of rhinoconjunctivitis in children between 18 and 36 months of age (adjusted RR 0.87; 95% CI 0.78-0.98) compared with no consumption during pregnancy. Maternal history of allergic disease did not influence this association.

Consumption, 3 times daily for 28 weeks, of a cow's milk-based drink containing docosahexaenoic acid, prebiotics polydextrose and galactooligosaccharides, yeast β-glucan, and micronutrients (zinc, vitamin A and iron) reduced episodes of allergic symptoms in a Brazilian RCT of 256 healthy 1- to 4-year-old children in day care.

Based on a survey of 143,967 children from 11 Latin-American countries, rhinoconjunctivitis was statistically negatively associated with fruit intake (OR 0.72; 95% CI 0.64-0.82) and positively associated with fast food/burger intake.
Diagnosis is made by a thorough history and physical examination, with ocular itching (especially in a patient with other allergies )being the hallmark of the condition. C

Differential.Differential_Features: History of medication use (i.e., dupilumab, opthalmic preparation for viral conjunctivitis)
Mucopurulent or purulent discharge; often begins as unilateral; eyes glued shut
Watery discharge without itching; tender periauricular node
Unilateral, visual confirmation, resolves with removal

list.listitem: Ocular symptoms, usually bilateral, including: itching (hallmark of allergic conjunctivitis), burning, and watering.
Associated with an allergic history.
Triggers: pollen from trees, grass, weeds, and pet dander.
May be seasonal or perennial.
Consider VKC in patients who report photophobia in addition to tearing, itching and burning.
Physical examination reveals redness and possibly mild conjunctival swelling (chemosis); allergic "shiners" (dark circles beneath the eyes) may be present due to vascular congestion.
Patients with VKC classically have giant papillae (cobblestone appearance) seen most commonly on the upper tarsal conjunctiva after lid eversion. The cornea may be involved with erosions or ulcers.
Diagnostic tests are not needed for the diagnosis of allergic conjunctivitis.

If bacterial conjunctivitis is suspected based on symptoms, especially eyes “glued shut” on awakening, treat with topical antibiotics to shorten the duration of illness; obtain cultures if neonatal conjunctivitis or suspected gonococcal conjunctivitis in any age group. Based on a systematic review, lack of morning "glue eye," (LR 0.3; 0.1-0.8) or failure to observe a red eye at 20 feet (LR 0.2; 0-0.8) may be useful for ruling out a bacterial cause of red eye.
Obtain smears for direct fluorescence antibody and Gram stain of conjunctival exudate to assess for intracellular gram-negative diplococci in cases of neonatal conjunctivitis.
Take the history and perform a comprehensive eye examination.
Rule out other causes of conjunctivitis.

In patients with red eye, photophobia via pupillary constriction and the presence of anisocoria >1 mm are the best predictors of serious eye disease such as uveitis, keratitis, or scleritis and requires prompt referral.
Testing is rarely necessary.

Topical antihistamines or mast cell stabilizers are effective for the treatment of allergic conjunctivitis as are intranasal steroids. A
These are also first-line agents for vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).
Systemic antihistamines are generally reserved for patients with atopic symptoms affecting other organ systems. C
Sublingual immunotherapy may provide some benefit. B
Clinical trials in allergic conjunctivitis are limited with respect to objective outcomes, disease relapse, and recurrence rates.

It is not clear that any nonsedating oral antihistamine, ophthalmic mast stabilizer, or ophthalmic antihistamine is more effective than any other for the treatment of allergic conjunctivitis. Therefore, treatment should be based on concomitant symptoms, convenience of use, cost, and patient preference (see ).
Topical mast cell stabilizers include cromolyn (Crolom), lodoxamide (Alomide), nedocromil (Alocril), and pemirolast (Alamast).

Topical antihistamines include emedastine (Emadine), levocabastine (Livostin), olopatadine (e.g., Patanol) and alcaftadine (Lastacaft); the latter is a once daily preparation. Comparative efficacy data are limited but authors of a systematic review found that olopatadine was inferior to alcaftadine with respect to ocular itch but comparable to epinastine and ketotifen and superior to placebo.
Dual antihistamine and mast cell stabilizers include azelastine (Optivar), epinastine (Elestat), ketotifen (Zaditor), olopatadine (Patanol), and bepotastine besilate (Bepreve).
Topical decongestants (naphazoline) and decongestant/antihistamine combinations (naphazoline/pheniramine) decrease erythema, congestion, and eyelid edema but can cause rebound hyperemia.
The topical nonsteroidal ketorolac (Acular) may also be used, but there are few data to support its use.

Topical corticosteroids use is limited since their use can increase intraocular pressure and cataract formation. There is potential for a single, physician-administered dexamethasone intracanalicular insert with favorable efficacy and safety data. Topical corticosteroids are effective for exacerbations of VKC.
Mast cell stabilizers, commonly cyclosporine and tacrolimus, were confirmed in a recent meta-analysis as first-line treatment for VKC.

Topical cyclosporine is more effective than placebo in reducing symptoms and topical steroid use in steroid-dependent allergic conjunctivitis. The most common side effect was a stinging or burning sensation upon use. In a case series of 30 patients with VKC who were resistant to first-line agents and corticosteroids, use of topical cyclosporine 0.05% resulted in improvement in signs and symptoms and reduction in use of steroids.

Topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, an immunosuppressive drug, reduced symptoms in 20 patients with resistant VKC who were followed for 2 years. Five patients discontinued the medication because of severe burning sensation. Symptoms returned on attempts to discontinue the medication. In an RCT of 40 consecutive patients with VKC in Iran randomized to either 0.005% tacrolimus or IFN alpha-2b (1,000,000 units/cc), signs and symptoms were similarly reduced in both treatment groups.

These agents decrease ocular symptoms in patients with allergic rhinitis and are a reasonable and safe alternative. Intranasal steroids are as effective (or better than) oral antihistamines in adults with allergic conjunctivitis.

In a single-blinded RCT of 150 children with pollen-related rhinoconjunctivitis, on-demand use of intranasal steroids or antihistamines was not inferior to daily use of intranasal steroids with respect to symptom-free days (30%, 15% and 7%, respectively). Patients randomized to on-demand steroid use averaged 61% less fluticasone than patients in the daily-intranasal steroid group.
Consider systemic antihistamines if patients have atopic symptoms affecting other organ systems.

The leukotriene receptor antagonist montelukast reduces ocular symptoms more than placebo but was not as effective as an oral antihistamine in adult patients. Montelukast was found to be safe and effective as a long-term therapy to prevent relapse in moderate to severe VKC.

IT has not been adequately studied in allergic conjunctivitis without nasal symptoms. Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 160 studies on allergic rhinitis found significant reductions in symptom (standardized mean differences [SMD] -0.53, 95% CI -0.63 to -0.42) and medication scores (SMD -0.37, 95% CI -0.49 to -0.26) while on IT treatment and possible continued benefits with respect to symptom scores after discontinuation of therapy. Duration of treatment varies. In an RCT comparing ultrashort ragweed IT, consisting of 4 weekly injections of active treatment, vs. placebo, IT was significantly more effective for total symptom scores with no serious adverse effects.

Authors of a Cochrane review and another systematic review found sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) reduced total ocular symptom scores and individual symptom scores for red eyes, itchy eyes and watery eyes compared to placebo but did not reduce use of ocular medication. In an RCT with 429 patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, investigators found ragweed SLIT to be more effective than placebo for combined daily rhinoconjunctivitis symptom and medication scores. The most recent meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found a small benefit of the grass pollen sublingual tablets, in reducing symptoms and decreasing use of symptomatic medication in patients with seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis but concluded that this small benefit did not justify its use.

Preseasonal SLIT treatment only, beginning either 2 or 4 months prior to pollen season, was better than placebo in one RCT. However, perennial IT appears to be more effective than preseasonal IT in the treatment of rhinoconjunctivitis in patients allergic to grass and rye pollens.

In children and adolescents with rhinoconjunctivitis, data are conflicting on benefit of SLIT. Authors of one systematic review found insufficient evidence that immunotherapy in any administration form had a positive effect on symptoms and/or medication use. However, in another systematic review of children, moderate evidence supported use of SLIT for reducing conjunctivitis symptoms and decreasing medication usage.

Intralymphatic immunotherapy (ILIT), a less time-consuming alternative to SLIT, was found to be better than placebo in reducing allergic symptoms in an RCT of 36 patients with pollen-induced rhinoconjunctivitis. In a systematic review with meta-analysis, ILIT was well tolerated and showed short-term benefits for seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, however long-term effects were inconclusive.

Probiotics Lactobacillus gasseri KS-13, Bifidobacterium bifidum G9-1, and B. longum MM-2 may improve rhinoconjunctivitis-specific quality of life during allergy season based on findings of a small RCT.
Allergen avoidance is the cornerstone of treatment.

In a case series of 15 children with severe allergic keratoconjunctivitis treated with bilateral supratarsal injection of triamcinolone acetonide, all patients showed significant symptomatic improvement and partial resolution within the first 2 weeks and only 6.7% of eyes had a severe relapse after a mean follow-up of 11 months. Ocular hypertension occurred in one of 20 children with VKC.

In experimentally-induced allergic conjunctivitis in 26 asymptomatic patients with proven seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, 2-week consumption of mandarin orange yogurt containing nobiletin and β-lactoglobulin significantly reduced symptom scores compared to the control yogurt group.
